items.stem: A 16-year-old boy has had high-arched feet, hammer toes, and frequent ankle sprains since childhood. His father has similar feet. Examination shows distal leg wasting and absent ankle reflexes. Motor conduction velocity in the median nerve is 24 m/s, uniformly slowed across all nerves tested, without conduction block. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Mutation of GJB1 on the X chromosome
items.explanation: Uniform severe slowing of conduction velocity below about 38 m/s with a dominant family history defines demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A, caused by a PMP22 duplication. A PMP22 deletion instead causes hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies and focal slowing at compression sites. MFN2 mutations cause an axonal form with near normal velocities. GJB1 causes an X-linked form with intermediate velocities, usually worse in men.

items.stem: Dozens of brief staring spells occur daily in a 7-year-old girl, each lasting about ten seconds with eyelid flutter, and she is unaware of them. Hyperventilation triggers an episode with 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges. She has never had a convulsion. Which is the best initial drug?
items.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy responds best to ethosuximide as first-line therapy when no generalized tonic-clonic seizures exist; a large randomized trial found it equal to valproate in seizure freedom with fewer attentional side effects. Valproate is reserved for patients who also have convulsions. Lamotrigine is less effective. Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures. Hyperventilation in the clinic often reproduces the discharges, which helps confirm the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows left facial numbness to pinprick, left Horner syndrome, left limb ataxia, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right arm and leg. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
items.explanation: Ipsilateral facial sensory loss, Horner syndrome, ataxia, and bulbar signs with contralateral body pain and temperature loss form the lateral medullary syndrome, usually from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery strokes cause facial weakness and hearing loss. Apical basilar infarcts cause somnolence and vertical gaze palsy. Posterior cerebral strokes cause visual field loss.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has dysarthria, a coarse tremor of the arms, and mood changes. Liver enzymes are mildly raised. Serum ceruloplasmin is low. Which examination finding would best confirm the underlying diagnosis?
options: Cherry red spot in the macula
items.explanation: Young onset movement disorder with psychiatric change, hepatic involvement, and low ceruloplasmin suggests Wilson disease, an ATP7B defect causing copper accumulation. Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination are present in nearly all patients with neurologic disease. A macular cherry red spot is seen in lysosomal storage disorders, retinal pigment loss in mitochondrial or peroxisomal disease, and lens subluxation in homocystinuria.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has severe vision loss in the right eye, then four weeks later a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning six segments. Aquaporin-4 antibody is positive. A neurologist considers a prior diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. Which disease modifying drug should be avoided?
items.explanation: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder with aquaporin-4 antibodies is an astrocytopathy that differs from multiple sclerosis. Interferon beta, natalizumab, fingolimod, and alemtuzumab can worsen it and should be avoided. Rituximab, satralizumab, eculizumab, inebilizumab, and azathioprine all reduce relapses and are used for prevention. Testing for aquaporin-4 antibody in atypical demyelination therefore prevents treatment that could cause disabling relapses.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has fluctuating confusion, well-formed visual hallucinations of children in his house, and mild parkinsonism. A trial of haloperidol caused severe rigidity and sedation. Which drug is most appropriate for the hallucinations and cognitive symptoms?
items.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies carries severe neuroleptic sensitivity, so typical and many atypical antipsychotics can cause rigidity, sedation, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine improve cognition and hallucinations and are first-line. Risperidone and olanzapine carry the same hazard, and memantine has weaker evidence for psychosis. Cholinesterase inhibitors are therefore preferred over antipsychotics in this disorder.

items.stem: A 20-month-old girl lost purposeful hand use and speech over four months. She now has constant hand wringing, acquired microcephaly, and episodes of breath holding. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Rett syndrome follows normal early development, then regression with loss of hand skills and speech, stereotypic hand wringing, breathing irregularities, and deceleration of head growth in a girl. It is caused by mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene. CDKL5 causes early onset epilepsy, SCN1A causes Dravet syndrome, and UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome with a happy demeanor.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought in with fever, rigidity, confusion, and a creatine kinase of 14,000 U/L three days after an increase in his antipsychotic dose. Pulse and blood pressure fluctuate. What is the most important initial step?
options: Add intravenous diazepam and continue the antipsychotic
Stop the antipsychotic and begin supportive cooling and hydration
Switch to a higher potency antipsychotic
items.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops with dopamine blockade and causes rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, and rhabdomyolysis. Management begins with discontinuing the drug, intensive supportive care, cooling, and fluids, with dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases. Continuing or intensifying dopamine blockade is dangerous. Cyproheptadine is used for serotonin syndrome, which presents with clonus. Monitoring creatinine and urine output is essential to prevent kidney injury from myoglobin.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man has had nightly attacks of severe right orbital pain for three weeks, each lasting 60 minutes with tearing and ptosis, and he paces during them. Sumatriptan injection aborts attacks. Which drug is the best preventive for this cycle?
items.explanation: Cluster headache is treated acutely with subcutaneous sumatriptan or high-flow oxygen, and verapamil is the first-line preventive. It can prolong PR interval, so electrocardiograms guide dose increases. Propranolol, amitriptyline, and topiramate are migraine preventives with weak evidence in cluster headache. Cardiac conduction should be checked because the drug can cause bradycardia and heart block, and treatment usually continues until the cluster period has ended.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has daily sleep attacks, sudden knee buckling when laughing, and vivid hallucinations as he falls asleep. Multiple sleep latency testing shows a mean latency of four minutes with three sleep onset REM periods. What is the underlying abnormality?
options: Reduced histamine release from the tuberomammillary nucleus
Loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the hypothalamus
Excess dopamine in the ventral tegmental area
Degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain
items.explanation: Narcolepsy type 1, with cataplexy and short REM latency, is caused by selective loss of hypocretin, also called orexin, neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, and cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin is low. This explains instability of the sleep wake switch and REM intrusion. Histamine, dopamine, and basal forebrain acetylcholine are not the primary defect. Sleep paralysis and fragmented nocturnal sleep complete the typical tetrad.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman is treated for severe hyponatremia of 104 mmol/L with hypertonic saline. Sodium rises to 120 mmol/L within 12 hours. Four days later she has dysarthria, dysphagia, and spastic quadriparesis. Which lesion is most likely on MRI?
options: Bilateral mesial temporal lobe signal change
items.explanation: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination, with a delayed biphasic course and classically pontine lesions leading to a locked-in picture. In high-risk patients the sodium rise should not exceed about 8 mmol/L per 24 hours. Mesial temporal changes suggest limbic encephalitis, mammillary body changes thiamine deficiency, and posterior edema hypertensive encephalopathy. Hypertonic saline and desmopressin strategies protect against overcorrection in high-risk patients.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count of 40 per microliter has two weeks of headache and vomiting. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 42 cm of water, and cryptococcal antigen is positive. Besides antifungal induction therapy, what is the best management of the pressure?
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV often causes raised intracranial pressure from yeast obstructing arachnoid granulations. Repeated lumbar punctures remove fluid until pressures normalize and improve survival. Acetazolamide and corticosteroids worsened outcomes in trials. Shunting is reserved for persistent high pressure despite serial drainage. The goal is to lower pressure by about half, repeating daily until it stays controlled.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends his neck. He has burning hands, severe weakness of both arms with relatively preserved leg strength, and urinary retention. MRI shows cord edema without fracture. Which syndrome is this?
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury in a spondylotic neck is the classic cause of central cord syndrome, where the medially placed arm fibers of the corticospinal tracts suffer more than leg fibers, giving disproportionate upper limb weakness with variable bladder dysfunction. Brown-Sequard is a hemisection with ipsilateral motor loss and contralateral pain loss. Anterior cord syndrome spares vibration. Posterior cord syndrome affects proprioception.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has a sudden sense that the room is spinning for 30 seconds each time she rolls over in bed. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right provokes upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short delay that fatigues. Hearing is normal. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with latent, fatigable upbeating torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike is posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, caused by displaced otoconia. Repositioning maneuvers cure most patients quickly. Vestibular suppressants delay central compensation and do not remove debris. Intratympanic steroids treat sudden hearing loss or Meniere disease, which would not be so positional. Success rates are high after one or two sessions.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with a newly resected glioblastoma, IDH wildtype, begins radiation with concurrent temozolomide. Which tumor marker best predicts benefit from temozolomide?
items.explanation: Methylation of the MGMT promoter silences a DNA repair enzyme that removes alkylation damage, so methylated tumors respond better to temozolomide. Codeletion of 1p and 19q defines oligodendroglioma and predicts chemotherapy sensitivity in that tumor type. IDH mutation marks lower grade astrocytomas and defines them separately from glioblastoma wildtype. MYCN amplification is a neuroblastoma and medulloblastoma marker.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has a stroke affecting the temporal lobe on the right. Visual field testing shows loss of the upper outer quadrants in both eyes on the left side. Which structure was most likely interrupted?
options: Dorsal optic radiation in the parietal lobe
Meyer loop of the optic radiation
items.explanation: Fibers from the inferior retina, representing the upper visual field, loop forward through the temporal lobe in Meyer loop before reaching the lower bank of the calcarine cortex. Damage causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, sometimes called pie in the sky. Parietal lesions cause an inferior quadrantanopia. A chiasmal lesion produces bitemporal loss, and a geniculate lesion produces a congruous defect often with a sectoral pattern.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has progressive axial stiffness, painful spasms triggered by sudden noise, and a rigid lumbar spine. She also has type 1 diabetes. Anti-GAD65 antibody titer is very high. Which drug is the best symptomatic treatment?
items.explanation: Stiff person syndrome produces fluctuating truncal and proximal limb rigidity with startle triggered spasms, linked to anti-GAD65 antibodies and other autoimmune disease. Benzodiazepines enhance gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling and are first-line, with baclofen as an adjunct. Pyridostigmine treats neuromuscular junction disease. Levodopa has no benefit, and phenytoin does not relieve spasm. Treatment may be combined with immunotherapy when symptoms are severe.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease has a standing blood pressure drop of 40 mm Hg systolic with lightheadedness, and midodrine is started. Which adverse effect requires specific monitoring?
items.explanation: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson disease is treated with midodrine, droxidopa, or fludrocortisone after nonpharmacologic measures. These pressors can cause supine hypertension because the baroreflex is impaired, so the last dose is taken several hours before bed and the head of the bed is raised. Hypoglycemia and hyperthermia are not expected effects, and the problem at night is elevated rather than reduced pressure.

items.stem: A 31-year-old graduate student wakes with a foot drop after sitting cross-legged for hours. He recalls two earlier episodes of a numb, weak hand after leaning on his elbow, each resolving over weeks. Nerve conduction studies show mildly slowed velocities across multiple nerves and focal slowing at the fibular head and elbow. Which finding would confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Recurrent painless pressure palsies at common entrapment sites with a diffuse mild demyelinating background indicate hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, caused by a PMP22 deletion. The duplication of the same gene produces the classic progressive Charcot-Marie-Tooth phenotype. Anti-MAG neuropathy is a slowly progressive sensory ataxic disorder in older men, and raised cerebrospinal protein would point to an acquired inflammatory neuropathy.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with generalized epilepsy has been seizure free on valproate for a year. Lamotrigine is added for better control and the starting dose is chosen. Why must the lamotrigine dose be lower and titrated more slowly than usual?
options: Valproate induces cytochrome P450 enzymes and lowers its level
Lamotrigine accumulates through renal tubular blockade
items.explanation: Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and roughly doubles the half-life of lamotrigine, increasing the risk of serious rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, if the usual titration is used. Valproate is not an enzyme inducer; inducers such as carbamazepine lower lamotrigine levels. The interaction is metabolic, not through protein binding displacement or renal tubular handling. Slow titration and a lower target dose reduce the rash risk.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman, three weeks postpartum, has a progressive headache, a focal seizure, and right arm weakness. Noncontrast CT shows a small left frontal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance venography shows absent flow in the superior sagittal sinus. What is the best treatment?
options: Acetazolamide alone with serial lumbar punctures
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation, which is recommended even when a venous infarct has hemorrhagic transformation, since the hemorrhage results from venous congestion. Acute therapy usually may begin with parenteral anticoagulants, followed by oral agents. Surgery is for impending herniation. Corticosteroids lack benefit, and acetazolamide treats intracranial hypertension without clearing clot. Regular INR monitoring is needed to keep levels in the target range.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has taken metoclopramide for gastroparesis for four years. She now has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and choreiform finger movements that bother her. Metoclopramide is stopped. Which medication is approved for the persistent movement?
items.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia follows prolonged dopamine receptor blockade, and metoclopramide is a common culprit. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors, valbenazine and deutetrabenazine, reduce the movements. Haloperidol would suppress them temporarily but worsen the underlying supersensitivity. Anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia, and levodopa does not treat choreic orofacial movements. Stopping the offending drug alone often does not resolve the movements, so treatment is added.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis has a three-day onset of left leg weakness and numbness. MRI shows a new enhancing thoracic lesion, and infection is excluded. Which treatment shortens the relapse?
options: Oral prednisone 20 mg daily for four weeks
Methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three to five days
Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g per kg for five days
items.explanation: High-dose corticosteroids speed recovery from a multiple sclerosis relapse, though they do not change long-term disability. The usual regimen is intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three to five days, with oral equivalents acceptable. Low-dose oral courses are inadequate. Immunoglobulin lacks proven benefit in acute relapses, and cyclophosphamide carries toxicity unsuited to a single relapse.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man becomes disinhibited, develops a sweet food craving, and stops showing concern for his wife. His brother has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. MRI shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which gene is the most likely cause in this family?
items.explanation: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia overlapping with motor neuron disease in a family points to a hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72, the most common genetic cause of both. APP and PSEN1 mutations cause early onset familial Alzheimer disease with amnestic presentation. The APOE e4 allele is a susceptibility factor for late onset Alzheimer disease, not a deterministic cause.

items.stem: A 5-month-old girl has clusters of flexor spasms and hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalography. Examination shows hypopigmented macules and an echogenic cardiac mass. Which is the most effective first-line drug for her spasms?
items.explanation: Infantile spasms with skin macules and cardiac rhabdomyomas point to tuberous sclerosis complex. Vigabatrin, which raises gamma-aminobutyric acid by inhibiting its breakdown, is preferred for spasms in this condition, with adrenocorticotropic hormone as an alternative. Phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine do not treat spasms effectively, and carbamazepine may worsen them. Treatment should start promptly because prolonged hypsarrhythmia worsens developmental outcome.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman starts linezolid for a wound infection while taking sertraline. Within hours she has agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, tremor, and inducible ankle clonus with hyperreflexia. Temperature is 38.9 C. Which drug is the appropriate antidote?
items.explanation: Serotonin syndrome follows combinations of serotonergic drugs, including linezolid, which inhibits monoamine oxidase, with an antidepressant. Clonus and hyperreflexia, especially in the legs, separate it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome. After stopping the agents and giving benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist, may be added. Dantrolene and bromocriptine treat other hyperthermic syndromes, and naloxone reverses opioids. The syndrome usually resolves within a day or two once the drugs are withdrawn.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has had a continuous right-sided headache for five months, with superimposed exacerbations that cause conjunctival injection and tearing. She has no remission periods. Sumatriptan and verapamil gave no relief. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanation: Continuous unilateral headache with trigeminal autonomic features and exacerbations is hemicrania continua, defined by an absolute response to indomethacin, with gastric protection advised. Oxygen and sumatriptan treat cluster attacks, not this continuous pattern. Lithium and verapamil are used for cluster prevention. Carbamazepine is used for trigeminal neuralgia, which causes brief shocks without autonomic signs or continuous baseline pain.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with unpleasant leg sensations in the evening, relieved by walking, has taken pramipexole for three years. Symptoms now start at midday, involve his arms, and are more severe than before the drug. What is the best management?
options: Taper the agonist and start pregabalin
Increase the pramipexole dose at bedtime
Add a second dopamine agonist at night
Start oral iron regardless of ferritin
items.explanation: Earlier daily onset, spread to the arms, and greater severity after long dopaminergic therapy describe augmentation of restless legs syndrome. Management is lowering or stopping the dopamine agonist and starting gabapentin, pregabalin, or gabapentin enacarbil. Raising the dose or adding another agonist worsens augmentation. Iron is given when ferritin is low, not regardless of level.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with severe hyperemesis gravidarum for eight weeks has confusion, nystagmus, and ataxia. She is about to receive intravenous dextrose. What should happen first?
options: A head CT before any treatment
items.explanation: Prolonged vomiting and poor intake cause thiamine deficiency, and the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia indicates Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamine must precede glucose because dextrose can precipitate or worsen the syndrome. Folate and B12 do not treat it, magnesium is a cofactor but not a substitute, and imaging should not delay treatment. Treatment continues with several days of high-dose thiamine.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has lancinating leg pains, loss of vibration and position sense with a positive Romberg sign, and small irregular pupils that constrict with accommodation but not to light. Serum treponemal testing is positive. Which treatment is recommended?
options: Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days
Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin
items.explanation: Tabes dorsalis with Argyll Robertson pupils indicates neurosyphilis, a tertiary form affecting the dorsal columns. Cerebrospinal fluid examination confirms involvement, and intravenous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days reaches treponemicidal levels in the central nervous system. A single benzathine dose does not penetrate adequately. Doxycycline and short ceftriaxone courses are alternatives only when penicillin cannot be used.

items.stem: Following a forward fall that hyperextended his neck, a 68-year-old man with known cervical spondylosis has weakness and numbness. He has arm weakness greater than leg weakness, hand numbness, and urinary retention. Which statement about his prognosis is most accurate?
options: Hand function typically recovers before leg function
Leg and bladder function typically recover before hand function
Complete recovery within hours is expected in all cases
Pain and temperature are preserved while strength is lost permanently
items.explanation: Arm-predominant weakness after hyperextension in a stenotic canal is central cord syndrome. The corticospinal fibers to the arms lie medially and are damaged first, while leg fibers are lateral and spared. Recovery generally follows the order of legs, bladder, then proximal arms, with hand dexterity returning least. Recovery is incomplete in many older patients, and sensory loss is variable.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a throbbing headache followed by drooping of the right eyelid. The right eye is deviated down and out and the right pupil is dilated and poorly reactive. What is the best next step?
options: Hemoglobin A1c measurement with outpatient follow-up
Urgent computed tomography angiography of the head
Temporal artery biopsy before any imaging
items.explanation: A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil and headache points to compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proved otherwise. Pupillomotor fibers run superficially and are affected first, so urgent vascular imaging is required. Microvascular palsies from diabetes typically spare the pupil. Edrophonium testing evaluates myasthenia, which spares the pupil, and arteritis does not cause this pattern.

items.stem: Over 3 weeks, an immunocompetent 62-year-old man develops confusion and apathy. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum. There is no herniation. What is the best next step?
options: Stereotactic biopsy, withholding corticosteroids if possible
Dexamethasone for 2 weeks to shrink the lesion and then biopsy
Whole brain radiotherapy started at once without tissue confirmation
items.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing deep lesion crossing the corpus callosum in an immunocompetent adult suggests primary central nervous system lymphoma. Corticosteroids are lymphocytotoxic and can shrink the tumor, making the biopsy nondiagnostic, so they are withheld unless herniation threatens. Treatment is based on tissue, with high-dose methotrexate as the backbone. Empiric toxoplasmosis therapy applies to patients with advanced HIV infection.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a right inferior quadrantanopia after a stroke. Which location best explains this deficit?
options: The left temporal lobe Meyer loop fibers
items.explanation: Fibers from the superior retina, carrying the inferior visual field, run in the parietal portion of the optic radiations, so a left parietal lesion causes a right inferior quadrantanopia. Lesions of the temporal Meyer loop affect inferior retinal fibers and cause a superior defect, the so-called pie in the sky. An optic tract lesion produces a complete homonymous hemianopia, and a chiasmal lesion causes bitemporal loss.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 2 weeks of agitation and delusions, followed by seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and a drop in oxygen saturation requiring intubation. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and magnetic resonance imaging is normal. Which test should be performed alongside immunotherapy?
options: Chest computed tomography for small-cell lung cancer
Testicular ultrasound for germ cell tumor
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasound for ovarian teratoma
items.explanation: Psychiatric onset followed by seizures, dyskinesias, and central hypoventilation in a young woman is classic for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Ovarian teratoma is the most common tumor association, and its removal improves outcome, so pelvic imaging is required. Small-cell lung cancer associates with other paraneoplastic syndromes, and testicular tumors apply to men. Breast cancer is linked to different antibodies.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man has difficulty releasing his grip on a doorknob, drooping eyelids, and frontal balding. His mother had cataract surgery at 45. Percussion of the thenar eminence causes a sustained dimple. He asks which routine surveillance he needs most. What is the best recommendation?
options: Yearly echocardiography for aortic root dilation
items.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1, a CTG repeat expansion in DMPK, is a multisystem disease. Cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias cause sudden death, so regular electrocardiograms and, when indicated, device implantation are central. Aortic root dilation is a Marfan concern. Creatine kinase is only mildly raised and does not guide care. Colorectal cancer screening follows average-risk guidance rather than a disease-specific schedule.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry has newly diagnosed focal epilepsy and carbamazepine is planned. Which pretreatment test reduces his risk of a severe cutaneous reaction?
items.explanation: HLA-B*1502 strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in people of Southeast Asian ancestry, so testing is recommended before starting and an alternative is chosen if positive. HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity. Thiopurine methyltransferase guides azathioprine dosing, and CYP2D6 genotyping informs other drug choices rather than carbamazepine safety. Carriers are usually offered an alternative drug such as levetiracetam.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman has three transient episodes of tingling that spreads across the right hand and face over minutes. She then has an acute lobar hemorrhage in the left parietal region. Gradient echo MRI shows multiple microbleeds restricted to cortical and subcortical regions. What is the most likely cause?
options: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
items.explanation: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy deposits beta amyloid in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels, causing recurrent lobar hemorrhages, convexity subarachnoid bleeding, and transient focal neurologic episodes sometimes called amyloid spells. Hypertensive microbleeds favor deep structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons. Multiple cavernous malformations show a popcorn pattern. Vasculitis has inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid and vessel wall changes.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has two years of lightheadedness on standing, urinary retention, violent dream enactment, and a slow shuffling gait. A trial of levodopa at 800 mg daily gave little benefit. Examination shows cerebellar dysarthria and laryngeal stridor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Early severe autonomic failure, REM sleep behavior disorder, poor levodopa response, cerebellar signs, and stridor characterize multiple system atrophy, an alpha-synucleinopathy with glial cytoplasmic inclusions. Parkinson disease with dementia responds to levodopa and has later autonomic changes. Progressive supranuclear palsy features early falls and vertical gaze palsy. Corticobasal syndrome causes asymmetric apraxia and cortical sensory loss.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has taken natalizumab for 30 months. She now has subacute right hemiparesis and visual neglect. MRI shows a nonenhancing subcortical white matter lesion with no mass effect. Which factor most increased her risk for this complication?
options: Previous Epstein-Barr virus infection with high titers
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from JC virus reactivation is the dangerous complication of natalizumab. Risk rises with anti-JC virus seropositivity, treatment longer than two years, and prior immunosuppressant use, with higher antibody index adding to the risk. Epstein-Barr titers, interferon beta use, and young age are not recognized predictors. Stratifying risk this way guides decisions about continuing treatment.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman has a year of magnetic gait with short steps, new urinary urgency, and slowed thinking. CT shows enlarged ventricles disproportionate to sulcal atrophy. After a high-volume lumbar puncture, her gait is much faster and steadier. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: Gait apraxia, urgency, and cognitive slowing with ventriculomegaly make normal pressure hydrocephalus likely, and gait improvement after a large-volume tap predicts shunt response. Shunting is the definitive therapy. Cholinesterase inhibitors treat degenerative dementia. Repeated punctures are only a diagnostic or temporary measure, and acetazolamide has not demonstrated durable benefit. Selection also relies on the clinical triad and imaging, and benefit is greater when gait is the main symptom.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has progressive gait ataxia, areflexia, scoliosis, and loss of vibration sense over four years. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. He is found to have a GAA repeat expansion. Which biochemical defect underlies this disease?
options: Defective vitamin E transport by TTPA
Impaired phytanic acid oxidation in peroxisomes
Faulty DNA repair from ATM mutation
items.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder that reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein, causing iron accumulation and oxidative damage. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes are typical. Vitamin E deficiency ataxia has a similar neurologic picture without a repeat expansion. Refsum disease involves phytanic acid, and ataxia telangiectasia involves ATM and telangiectasias. Cardiomyopathy is the usual cause of death, so regular cardiac assessment is important.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman takes lithium for bipolar disorder. She has a fine postural tremor, polyuria with intense thirst, and a urine osmolality that stays low after desmopressin. Which complication does this represent?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
items.explanation: Lithium impairs collecting duct response to antidiuretic hormone, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, shown by failure of urine to concentrate after desmopressin. A fine postural tremor is a common benign effect. Central diabetes insipidus would respond to desmopressin. Toxicity usually brings coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion, and inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion causes retention of water, not polyuria.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a headache that appears within minutes of standing and clears when she lies flat. She has neck stiffness and muffled hearing. MRI shows diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and brain sagging. Bed rest and caffeine failed. What is the best next treatment?
options: Lumbar puncture drainage of cerebrospinal fluid
items.explanation: Orthostatic headache with pachymeningeal enhancement and brain sag signals spontaneous intracranial hypotension, caused by a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Conservative therapy comes first, and an epidural blood patch, repeated if necessary, is the standard next step. Removing more fluid worsens the leak, acetazolamide lowers fluid production in the wrong clinical setting, and antibiotics address meningitis. Most patients improve, though a second patch is sometimes needed.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy has excessive daytime sleepiness since age 14, brief episodes of knee buckling when he laughs, and vivid hallucinations as he falls asleep. Which abnormality underlies this disorder?
options: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
Loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain
Loss of hypocretin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus
Dysfunction of serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe
items.explanation: Daytime sleepiness with cataplexy and hypnagogic hallucinations defines narcolepsy type 1. It results from loss of hypocretin-producing cells in the lateral hypothalamus, with low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin-1 and a link to HLA DQB1*06:02. Dopaminergic loss in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson disease, and cholinergic basal forebrain loss is part of Alzheimer disease. Raphe dysfunction does not explain cataplexy.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C has 3 days of day-night reversal, confusion, and asterixis. There is no gastrointestinal bleeding or infection. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Restriction of dietary protein to 0.5 g per kg daily for 2 weeks
Lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools daily
items.explanation: Asterixis and altered sleep-wake cycle in cirrhosis indicate hepatic encephalopathy, caused by ammonia and other gut-derived toxins. Lactulose lowers ammonia absorption, and the dose is titrated to stool frequency, with rifaximin added to prevent recurrence. Protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is no longer advised. Flumazenil is not standard therapy, and mannitol is for cerebral edema in acute liver failure.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man from a rural area has a first generalized seizure. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a single 1 cm cystic lesion with an eccentric dot inside and mild surrounding edema. Which treatment is best?
options: Albendazole with a corticosteroid and an antiseizure medication
Surgical excision of the cyst through craniotomy
Antiseizure medication alone with no other treatment
items.explanation: A cyst with an eccentric scolex is the classic image of viable neurocysticercosis, the leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions. Albendazole kills the larvae, and corticosteroids are given with it to blunt the inflammatory response to dying cysts. An antiseizure drug controls the seizures. Surgery is reserved for obstructive or intraventricular cysts, and steroids or seizure control alone leave the parasite untreated.

items.stem: A 16-year-old football player had a concussion with headache and dizziness, and both resolved at rest 3 days later. His neurologic examination is normal. Which plan is best for returning to sport?
options: Full contact practice as soon as the headache has resolved
A stepwise return-to-play progression once he is symptom free
Two weeks of strict rest in a quiet darkened room with no screens
A head computed tomography scan before any activity
items.explanation: After concussion, symptoms usually resolve within days to weeks. Current guidance favors brief initial rest followed by gradual activity, with a staged return from light aerobic exercise to full contact only when the athlete remains symptom free at each level. Premature return risks prolonged symptoms. Prolonged strict rest delays recovery, and imaging is unnecessary when there are no red flags.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has brief spinning lasting under a minute when she rolls over in bed. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right produces upbeating torsional nystagmus after a latency that fatigues on repetition. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with latent, fatiguing torsional upbeat nystagmus on Dix-Hallike testing indicates posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. The Epley maneuver moves displaced otoconia out of the canal and cures most patients in one or two sessions. Vestibular suppressants only mask symptoms and slow compensation. Intratympanic gentamicin is a destructive procedure reserved for refractory Meniere disease.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man reports six years of trouble gripping a pen and buttoning shirts, and recent falls because his knees buckle. Examination shows atrophy of the forearm flexors and quadriceps with mild dysphagia. Creatine kinase is slightly elevated. Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and endomysial inflammation. What is the most appropriate management?
items.explanation: Selective finger flexor and quadriceps weakness with rimmed vacuoles characterizes inclusion body myositis. Despite inflammatory infiltrates, it does not respond meaningfully to corticosteroids, other immunosuppressants, or immunoglobulin in trials, so management is supportive, with exercise, assistive devices, and dysphagia care. Treatments that help polymyositis and dermatomyositis expose patients to risk without benefit here. Supportive care is the standard, and early physiotherapy with swallowing precautions reduces complications.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had focal impaired awareness seizures with rising epigastric sensation for six years despite adequate trials of lamotrigine and levetiracetam. MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis, concordant with video-electroencephalography. What is the best next step?
options: Repeating the MRI in one year
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance of freedom with a third drug is low. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with concordant hippocampal sclerosis has high surgical success, and a randomized trial showed surgery beat continued medication. Dietary therapy is more typical in children, and delaying with repeat imaging adds risk, including sudden unexpected death.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had one episode of left monocular visual loss lasting five minutes. Computed tomography angiography shows 80 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery with a smooth plaque. He has no disabling deficits. What is the best management?
options: Carotid stenting after six months of therapy
items.explanation: Symptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99 percent carries a high early recurrence risk, and endarterectomy gives the greatest benefit when done within about two weeks of the event in surgical candidates, alongside antiplatelet and statin therapy. Delaying for months wastes the period of highest risk. Thrombolysis is for disabling acute ischemic stroke, not a resolved transient event. Bypass has no proven role in carotid disease.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with chorea, depression, and a father who developed similar symptoms at age 58 asks about her risk. Her father's disease began later than his own father's. Which statement about the transmission pattern is correct?
options: Expansion occurs only through maternal transmission
The repeat shortens in each generation
CAG expansion is likelier through the father
Inheritance follows an X-linked recessive pattern
items.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder in HTT. Repeats are unstable and tend to expand when passed by fathers, producing anticipation, which means earlier onset in later generations. Maternal transmission is less prone to large expansion. Shortening would reduce penetrance, and the pattern is autosomal rather than X-linked. Genetic counseling should explain this pattern to at-risk relatives.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has fever, then ataxia, irritability, and left arm weakness two weeks after an upper respiratory infection. MRI shows large, poorly marginated bilateral white matter lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. What is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a monophasic, postinfectious demyelinating illness with multifocal, large lesions and encephalopathy. First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids, with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange reserved for failure. Acyclovir may be given while herpes encephalitis is excluded but is not the definitive therapy. Antiseizure drugs and interferon beta treat other conditions. Early treatment limits residual deficits, and most children recover well.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman has rapidly progressive dementia over three months, with startle myoclonus and ataxia. Diffusion MRI shows cortical ribboning and restricted diffusion in the caudate. Which cerebrospinal fluid test is the most sensitive and specific?
options: Phosphorylated tau to total tau ratio
items.explanation: Rapid dementia with myoclonus and cortical ribbon diffusion restriction suggests sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The real-time quaking-induced conversion assay detects misfolded prion protein and has high sensitivity and specificity, outperforming the older 14-3-3 test. Amyloid and tau markers support Alzheimer disease, and oligoclonal bands indicate intrathecal inflammation. Earlier diffusion MRI changes support the diagnosis, but cerebrospinal fluid confirmation is preferred when available.

items.stem: A 6-month-old boy with two copies of the SMN2 gene and a homozygous SMN1 deletion is diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy. His parents ask what predicts how severe the disease will be. What is the best answer?
options: The size of the SMN1 deletion
The age of the mother at conception
The level of serum creatine kinase
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from loss of SMN1, and SMN2 produces a small amount of functional protein. More SMN2 copies lead to milder disease, so copy number is the main modifier and guides treatment decisions. Deletion size does not correlate with severity, maternal age is unrelated to an inherited recessive disease, and creatine kinase is normal or mildly raised.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman taking sertraline is started on linezolid for a skin infection. Within a day she has agitation, diarrhea, temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius, tremor, inducible clonus, and brisk reflexes. What is the best management?
options: Give intravenous dantrolene and apply external cooling
Stop the serotonergic agents and give cyproheptadine
items.explanation: Clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, and fever developing hours after combining a serotonergic antidepressant with linezolid, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, indicate serotonin syndrome. Treatment is withdrawal of the offending drugs, supportive cooling, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist, for moderate cases. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and haloperidol may worsen the picture.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has nightly attacks of severe left orbital pain lasting about 90 minutes, with tearing, nasal congestion, and restlessness, occurring for 5 weeks. Which preventive drug should be started?
options: Propranolol titrated to the maximal tolerated dose
Sumatriptan taken daily for the whole cluster period
items.explanation: Short, severe unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic features and agitation, recurring in a cluster, define cluster headache. Verapamil is the first-line preventive, and an electrocardiogram is needed because high doses can prolong the PR interval. Beta blockers and tricyclic drugs have little evidence here. Triptans are for acute attacks and are limited in frequency, so daily use for prevention is not appropriate.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks of pregnancy has evening leg discomfort relieved by walking and worse at rest. Examination is normal and ferritin is 28 ng/mL. What is the best management?
options: Bedtime pramipexole at the lowest available dose, titrated upward
Oral iron supplementation to raise ferritin above 75 ng/mL
items.explanation: Evening urge to move the legs, relieved by movement, defines restless legs syndrome, and low brain iron is a major driver. Iron repletion is first-line when ferritin is below about 75 ng/mL, and is especially suitable in pregnancy. Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole can cause augmentation with long-term use and are poor first choices. Gabapentin enacarbil is an alternative but is not preferred during pregnancy.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has 6 months of foot numbness and gait unsteadiness. Examination shows loss of vibration and position sense in the legs, positive Romberg sign, and brisk knee reflexes. Hemoglobin is normal and B12 is borderline. Which test best clarifies the diagnosis?
options: Serum folate level with red cell folate
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
items.explanation: Dorsal column loss with hyperreflexia suggests subacute combined degeneration from cobalamin deficiency, which can occur before anemia appears. When serum B12 is borderline, elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm functional deficiency. Folate deficiency does not usually cause myelopathy. Copper deficiency can mimic this picture, but it is considered after B12 is addressed. Sedimentation rate does not help localize this process.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has two years of difficulty climbing stairs and morning headaches. Forced vital capacity falls from 2.9 L upright to 1.8 L supine. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and biopsy shows vacuoles containing glycogen. Which therapy targets the underlying defect?
items.explanation: Late-onset Pompe disease, from acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, presents with proximal limb girdle weakness and early diaphragm involvement, shown by a large drop in supine vital capacity. Enzyme replacement therapy slows respiratory and motor decline. Carnitine deficiency and mitochondrial myopathy do not store lysosomal glycogen. Pyridostigmine treats neuromuscular junction disorders, which would not produce vacuolar glycogen biopsy changes.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has repeated 20-minute episodes of whole-body shaking with eyes tightly closed throughout, starting after an assault. The episodes occur in the waiting room and have not responded to three antiseizure drugs. Serum lactate is normal afterward. What is the best diagnostic step?
options: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology
Empiric trial of a fourth antiseizure drug
items.explanation: Prolonged events with sustained eye closure, waxing and waning movements, and failure of multiple drugs suggest functional seizures, but the diagnosis is confirmed by capturing a typical event on video-electroencephalography without epileptiform activity. Normal lactate supports but does not prove it. A routine recording may be normal in either condition, and further drugs expose her to harm if the diagnosis is wrong.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an over-the-counter nasal decongestant has recurrent thunderclap headaches over ten days. Neurologic examination is normal and initial CT is normal. Catheter angiography shows segmental narrowing and dilation of multiple arteries. Which step is most important?
options: Placing an intracranial stent in the narrowest vessel
items.explanation: Recurrent thunderclap headache with reversible multifocal vasoconstriction is reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, precipitated by serotonergic drugs, sympathomimetics, and the postpartum state. Management is withdrawal of triggers, blood pressure control, and often a calcium channel blocker. Corticosteroids have been associated with worse outcomes. Anticoagulation and stenting address thrombosis or fixed stenosis, not reversible spasm. Most patients recover over weeks once the triggering agents are removed.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has a toe-walking gait that worsens through the day and improves after sleep. Examination shows mild dystonia of the legs with brisk reflexes. Brain MRI is normal. A low dose of levodopa gives a dramatic, sustained response. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Diurnal fluctuation of dystonia that responds fully to small levodopa doses defines dopa-responsive dystonia, most often from dominant GCH1 mutations that reduce tetrahydrobiopterin and dopamine synthesis. ATP1A3 causes rapid-onset dystonia parkinsonism and alternating hemiplegia. PRRT2 causes paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia. SLC2A1 causes glucose transporter deficiency with seizures and exercise induced dyskinesia. Levodopa responsiveness is so complete that the treatment trial also confirms the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 2 weeks of progressive leg weakness, a sensory level, and urinary retention. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a T2 lesion spanning five vertebral segments, and aquaporin-4 antibody is positive. Which multiple sclerosis therapy should be avoided because it may worsen her disease?
items.explanation: A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis with aquaporin-4 antibody confirms neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Interferon beta, natalizumab, and fingolimod have been associated with worsening or increased relapses in this disorder. Inebilizumab, satralizumab, and eculizumab are approved targeted therapies for antibody-positive disease, acting on B cells, interleukin-6 signaling, and complement respectively. Early recognition of this disorder matters because the wrong choice can trigger severe relapses.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man shows fluctuating alertness, well-formed visual hallucinations of children, and mild bradykinesia that began after the cognitive symptoms. He is distressed by the hallucinations. Which medication is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism within a year of dementia indicate dementia with Lewy bodies. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine often reduce hallucinations and improve cognition, and they are tried first. Typical and many atypical antipsychotics, including haloperidol and risperidone, risk severe sensitivity reactions with worsened parkinsonism. Memantine has modest benefit and is not first-line for psychosis.

items.stem: A 15-month-old girl who had been using words and grasping toys now shows loss of purposeful hand use, constant hand wringing, and slowing of head growth. Which gene is most likely mutated?
options: FMR1 with a CGG repeat expansion
items.explanation: Normal early development followed by regression, loss of hand skills, stereotyped hand wringing, and deceleration of head growth in a girl define Rett syndrome. It is caused by MECP2 mutations, usually de novo and lethal or severe in males. UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome with happy demeanor and ataxia. SMN1 loss causes spinal muscular atrophy, and FMR1 expansion causes fragile X syndrome.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man with bipolar disorder who takes lithium reports vomiting, coarse tremor, and unsteady gait 5 days after another physician started a new medication. Which medication most likely precipitated this?
items.explanation: Coarse tremor, ataxia, and gastrointestinal symptoms indicate lithium toxicity. Lithium is cleared by the kidney, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs reduce clearance and raise levels. Acetaminophen, omeprazole, and metformin do not meaningfully alter renal lithium handling, although dehydration from any illness can contribute. Severe cases may require hemodialysis. Serum level and renal function guide management.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a body mass index of 36 reports daily headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, and brief visual obscurations. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema, magnetic resonance imaging is normal, and opening pressure is 38 cm of water. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Acetazolamide with a weight reduction program
Serial lumbar punctures as the sole treatment
items.explanation: Papilledema with normal imaging, elevated opening pressure, and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition in an obese young woman indicates idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The goal is to protect vision, and acetazolamide plus weight loss is the first-line approach. Repeated punctures give only transient relief. Furosemide is a weak alternative, and surgical fenestration is reserved for progressive visual loss despite medical therapy.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has noted tongue fasciculations, perioral twitching, slowly progressive proximal weakness, and cramps for eight years. He has gynecomastia and reduced fertility. Sensory nerve action potentials are low in amplitude. Which statement about the genetic cause is correct?
options: A GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72
A deletion of the SMN1 gene
CAG repeats in the androgen receptor
items.explanation: Kennedy disease, X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, results from a CAG expansion in the androgen receptor gene. Androgen insensitivity explains gynecomastia and infertility, and sensory involvement distinguishes it from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. C9orf72 and SOD1 variants cause familial motor neuron disease with upper motor neuron signs. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, usually in childhood.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has morning jerks of both arms that make her drop a cup, plus one generalized tonic-clonic seizure after a night of studying. Electroencephalography shows 4 to 6 Hz generalized polyspike and wave discharges with photic stimulation. Which drug is the best choice for long-term treatment?
items.explanation: Morning myoclonus, generalized seizures precipitated by sleep deprivation, and photosensitive polyspike discharges define juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. In a woman of childbearing potential, levetiracetam is a broad-spectrum agent with a favorable teratogenic profile, whereas valproate carries the highest fetal risk. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized epilepsy. Gabapentin has little efficacy in generalized syndromes.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking an oral contraceptive has 5 days of worsening headache, then a focal seizure of the right arm. Imaging shows a left parasagittal hemorrhagic venous infarct and a filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus on venography. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Withholding anticoagulation until the hemorrhage has fully resolved on repeat imaging
Aspirin alone to avoid worsening the bleeding
Therapeutic anticoagulation despite the intracranial hemorrhage
Immediate decompressive craniectomy for all patients
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis with a hemorrhagic infarct is still treated with anticoagulation, because the hemorrhage results from venous congestion and treating the clot improves outcome. Delaying therapy risks propagation of thrombus and further venous infarction. Antiplatelet therapy does not adequately treat venous thrombosis. Surgery is reserved for herniation or refractory intracranial pressure, not as a routine first step.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has 6 months of tremor on reaching, slurred speech, and personality change. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown corneal rings. Which mechanism underlies his disease?
options: Defective intestinal copper absorption from ATP7A dysfunction
Brain iron accumulation from pantothenate kinase deficiency
Excess ceruloplasmin synthesis from a regulatory mutation
Impaired biliary copper excretion from ATP7B dysfunction
items.explanation: Young-onset tremor, dysarthria, behavioral change, and Kayser-Fleischer rings indicate Wilson disease. Mutations in ATP7B impair copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and biliary excretion, leading to copper deposition in liver, basal ganglia, and cornea. ATP7A mutations cause Menkes disease in infants. Pantothenate kinase deficiency causes brain iron accumulation with the eye-of-the-tiger sign. Ceruloplasmin is typically low rather than excessive.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops confusion, ataxia, and irritability 2 weeks after a viral illness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows multifocal large T2 lesions in the white matter and thalami. After acute treatment, which statement about prognosis is most accurate?
options: Most children recover fully, and a monophasic course is typical
Most progress to multiple sclerosis within one year
Lifelong disease-modifying therapy is required in nearly all
Relapses occur every few months in most children
items.explanation: Encephalopathy with multifocal demyelination after infection is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, usually treated with intravenous methylprednisolone. The course is typically monophasic, and most children recover well. A minority later receive a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis or myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease. Maintenance therapy is therefore not routine, and frequent relapses are unusual. Brain lesions often resolve on follow-up imaging.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman has 1 year of short-stepped, wide-based gait with feet that seem stuck to the floor, urinary urgency, and mild forgetfulness. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulci. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt without further testing
Six-month trial of acetazolamide with repeat imaging at its end
Large-volume lumbar puncture with gait testing before and after
Brain biopsy of the frontal cortex to exclude prion disease
items.explanation: The triad of magnetic gait, urgency, and cognitive slowing with disproportionate ventriculomegaly suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus. A tap test removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, with objective gait comparison, helps predict shunt response and is performed before surgery. Shunting without selection exposes patients to complications. Acetazolamide has no proven role, and biopsy is unwarranted without rapid decline.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has seven light brown skin macules larger than 5 mm and freckling in both axillae. His examination is otherwise normal. Which surveillance measure is recommended for his childhood years?
options: Annual brain and spine magnetic resonance imaging in every child
Annual ophthalmologic examination for optic pathway glioma
Yearly audiometry for bilateral vestibular schwannoma screening
Yearly renal ultrasound screening for angiomyolipoma
items.explanation: Multiple cafe-au-lait macules with axillary freckling meet criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1. Optic pathway gliomas occur mostly before age 7, so regular visual and ophthalmologic assessment is advised. Routine imaging is reserved for symptoms. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2, and renal angiomyolipomas are a feature of tuberous sclerosis. Parents should also be taught to report new visual symptoms.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has sudden left leg weakness after a stressful event. When she flexes her right hip against the examiner's hand, her weak left hip extends with normal force against the examiner's other hand. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Upper motor neuron weakness from a cervical lesion
Lower motor neuron weakness from a lumbar radiculopathy
Hoover sign, which supports functional weakness
Myopathic weakness from inflammatory muscle disease
items.explanation: Involuntary hip extension of the weak leg during contralateral hip flexion, with a collapse of voluntary effort on direct testing, is the Hoover sign. It is a positive clinical sign of functional neurological disorder rather than a diagnosis of exclusion. Structural weakness would not recover with the automatic movement. Upper motor neuron, radicular, and myopathic weakness have objective signs such as spasticity, reflex loss, or elevated enzymes.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes reports 4 months of difficulty rising from chairs, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Examination shows proximal leg weakness with absent ankle reflexes that briefly return after 10 seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction. Which antibody is the likely cause?
options: Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Antibodies against the voltage-gated potassium channel complex
items.explanation: Proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and facilitation of reflexes after exercise define Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release, and small-cell lung cancer is the classic association in a smoker. Postsynaptic receptor and MuSK antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which fatigues without autonomic features or reflex facilitation. Potassium channel complex antibodies produce neuromyotonia or limbic encephalitis.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man weighing 80 kg is found seizing in a parking lot by paramedics who cannot place an intravenous line. The convulsion has lasted 6 minutes. Which first treatment is recommended?
items.explanation: Convulsive seizures lasting 5 minutes meet the operational definition of status epilepticus, and a benzodiazepine must be given at once. When intravenous access is unavailable, intramuscular midazolam is as effective as intravenous lorazepam and is the preferred route for adults above 40 kg. A convulsing patient cannot take oral drugs safely. Intramuscular phenytoin is absorbed erratically and is not used, and subcutaneous levetiracetam is not an established emergency route.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man develops left neck pain and a droopy eyelid after a violent coughing fit. Examination shows left ptosis and miosis with preserved sweating of the face. Where is the lesion?
options: First-order hypothalamic fibers in the lateral medulla
Second-order preganglionic fibers at the lung apex
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain
Third-order sympathetic fibers along the internal carotid artery
items.explanation: Neck pain with partial Horner syndrome suggests internal carotid dissection injuring the postganglionic sympathetic plexus wrapped around the artery. Facial sweating is spared because sudomotor fibers to most of the face travel with the external carotid. Central lesions in the lateral medulla and preganglionic lesions at the apex of the lung usually produce anhidrosis of the face. The Edinger-Westphal nucleus mediates pupillary constriction, so injury would cause mydriasis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for 12 years has rhythmic tongue protrusion and lip smacking. His psychiatrist wants to continue the antipsychotic. Which addition is best for his movements?
options: Benztropine, an anticholinergic agent at standard dose
Propranolol, a nonselective beta blocker at bedtime
Carbidopa and levodopa taken three times daily
items.explanation: Orofacial stereotypies after years of dopamine blockade are tardive dyskinesia. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine reduce dopamine release and are first-line treatment, without stopping a needed antipsychotic. Anticholinergic drugs may worsen tardive dyskinesia even though they help acute dystonia. Propranolol treats akathisia, and levodopa would increase dopaminergic stimulation and risk worsening the dyskinesia.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has received natalizumab for 30 months. He develops subacute right visual field loss and clumsiness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a nonenhancing subcortical white matter lesion, and cerebrospinal fluid is positive for JC virus by polymerase chain reaction. What is the best next step?
options: Stop natalizumab and consider plasma exchange to speed clearance
Continue natalizumab and add a prolonged course of high-dose corticosteroids
Switch to ocrelizumab or another potent immunosuppressant
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy complicates natalizumab, with risk rising with antibody positivity, prior immunosuppression, and treatment beyond 2 years. The drug must be stopped, and plasma exchange removes it faster. Corticosteroids are reserved for immune reconstitution syndrome. Another immunosuppressant would worsen JC virus control, and acyclovir has no activity against this polyomavirus. Early recognition improves the odds of survival with function.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has 2 years of disinhibition, eating only sweets, loss of empathy, and apathy, with preserved memory. Several relatives had dementia or motor neuron disease. Which genetic abnormality is the most common cause of familial disease in this syndrome?
options: A duplication of the amyloid precursor protein gene
A missense mutation in the presenilin 1 gene
A CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
A hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72
items.explanation: Early behavioral change, hyperorality, and relative memory sparing indicate behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia. Overlap with motor neuron disease in the family points to the C9orf72 repeat expansion, the most frequent genetic cause, with progranulin and tau mutations next. Amyloid precursor protein and presenilin 1 mutations produce early-onset Alzheimer disease, and huntingtin expansion causes Huntington disease.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls, calf enlargement, and needs to push on his thighs to stand. Creatine kinase is 22,000 units per liter, and genetic testing shows an out-of-frame exon deletion in the dystrophin gene. Which intervention slows loss of motor function?
items.explanation: Early-onset proximal weakness, Gowers maneuver, pseudohypertrophy, and very high creatine kinase with an out-of-frame deletion indicate Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Corticosteroids prolong ambulation and delay respiratory and cardiac decline, and are started before major decline. Dantrolene reduces calcium release for malignant hyperthermia, creatine lacks efficacy, and pyridostigmine treats neuromuscular junction disorders. Cardiac and respiratory monitoring continue alongside drug therapy.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops ascending leg weakness and numbness 10 days after a diarrheal illness. She cannot walk unaided, has absent reflexes, and cerebrospinal fluid shows 2 cells per microliter with protein of 110 mg/dL. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Intravenous immune globulin given daily for 5 days
Rituximab infusions repeated every 6 months for a year
Pyridostigmine titrated upward to control the weakness
items.explanation: Albuminocytologic dissociation with ascending areflexic weakness after infection indicates Guillain-Barre syndrome, and she is unable to walk, so immunotherapy is indicated. Intravenous immune globulin hastens recovery. Corticosteroids have not shown benefit in this disorder. Rituximab is used in other antibody-mediated neuropathies and myasthenia but lacks evidence in the acute setting. Pyridostigmine treats neuromuscular junction disease and does not alter this immune neuropathy.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has dozens of 10-second staring spells daily, provoked by hyperventilation, with 3 Hz generalized spike and wave discharges on electroencephalography. Which drug is most likely to worsen her seizures?
items.explanation: Typical absence seizures with 3 Hz spike and wave activity respond to ethosuximide, valproate, or lamotrigine, so these are not expected to worsen the disorder. Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures in generalized epilepsy syndromes, sometimes precipitating absence status. Recognition of the generalized pattern on electroencephalography therefore guides drug selection away from narrow-spectrum agents.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation has a minor ischemic stroke while taking aspirin daily. Renal function is normal and she has no bleeding history. Which change is best for secondary prevention?
options: Switch from aspirin to a direct oral anticoagulant
Continue aspirin and add clopidogrel for 3 years
Increase aspirin to 650 mg twice daily
Begin warfarin with a target international normalized ratio of 3.5 to 4.5
items.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes cardioembolic stroke, which antiplatelet therapy prevents poorly. Direct oral anticoagulants are at least as effective as warfarin, cause less intracranial hemorrhage, and need no monitoring. Dual antiplatelet therapy and higher aspirin doses add bleeding without adequate stroke protection. Warfarin is an acceptable agent only at a target international normalized ratio of 2 to 3, and a higher range increases hemorrhage.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has parkinsonism unresponsive to levodopa, early orthostatic hypotension, inspiratory stridor, and acting out dreams. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a cruciform signal in the pons. What pathology is expected?
options: Tau-positive tufted astrocytes in the midbrain tegmentum and subthalamic nucleus
Cortical neuronal Lewy bodies with diffuse amyloid plaques
Alpha-synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes
TDP-43 inclusions in frontal and temporal cortical neurons
items.explanation: Poor levodopa response, early autonomic failure, stridor, and the hot cross bun sign indicate multiple system atrophy. Its hallmark is glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein within oligodendrocytes. Tufted astrocytes are characteristic of progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy. Hot cross buns reflect pontocerebellar fiber loss. Cortical Lewy bodies mark dementia with Lewy bodies. TDP-43 inclusions characterize frontotemporal dementia and motor neuron disease.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis taking teriflunomide wishes to conceive within 6 months. Which step is most appropriate before conception?
options: Switching to fingolimod until the third trimester
Starting cladribine tablets a month before conception
items.explanation: Teriflunomide is teratogenic and persists in plasma for months to years because of enterohepatic recirculation. An accelerated elimination procedure with cholestyramine lowers levels below the safe threshold before conception. Continuing the drug exposes the fetus. Fingolimod and cladribine are not recommended in pregnancy, and cladribine in addition requires contraception during and after treatment. Planning should begin before drug selection.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man after a left hemispheric stroke speaks fluently with correct grammar, comprehends commands well, but cannot repeat the phrase he was given and makes phonemic errors. Which structure is most likely damaged?
options: The inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
The angular gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
The arcuate fasciculus and adjacent supramarginal gyrus
The watershed zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
items.explanation: Fluent speech with good comprehension but poor repetition and phonemic paraphasias is conduction aphasia, from disruption of the arcuate fasciculus linking temporal and frontal language regions, often with the supramarginal gyrus. Damage to the inferior frontal gyrus produces nonfluent Broca aphasia. Angular gyrus lesions cause alexia with agraphia. Watershed infarcts produce transcortical aphasias with intact repetition.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has grip myotonia, frontal balding, bilateral cataracts, and a father who had a pacemaker placed at age 45. Muscle biopsy is not planned because genetic testing is available. Which mechanism best explains his disease?
options: Toxic RNA gain of function sequestering splicing regulators such as MBNL1
Loss of dystrophin from the sarcolemma through a frameshift deletion
Loss of function of the skeletal muscle chloride channel gene
Gain of function of the skeletal muscle sodium channel gene
items.explanation: Myotonia with cataracts, frontal balding, and cardiac conduction disease is myotonic dystrophy type 1, caused by a CTG expansion in DMPK. The transcribed repeat RNA forms nuclear foci that sequester MBNL splicing proteins and disrupt splicing of many genes. Dystrophin loss causes Duchenne and Becker dystrophy. Chloride and sodium channel mutations produce myotonia congenita and paramyotonia without systemic features such as cataracts or conduction disease.

items.stem: A 5-month-old boy has clusters of flexor spasms on waking, developmental plateau, and several hypopigmented macules on the trunk. Electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia. Which first-line oral therapy is appropriate and carries a risk of peripheral visual field loss?
items.explanation: Spasm clusters, hypsarrhythmia, and ash leaf macules indicate infantile spasms from tuberous sclerosis complex. Vigabatrin is especially effective in this etiology, and its main risk is irreversible bilateral visual field constriction, so periodic assessment is needed. Phenobarbital and levetiracetam have little efficacy for this syndrome. Carbamazepine can worsen spasms and generalized epilepsies, and adrenocorticotropic hormone is the other first-line agent.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man taking warfarin has sudden headache and left hemiparesis. Computed tomography shows a 40 mL right basal ganglia hemorrhage, and the international normalized ratio is 3.8. Which reversal approach is best?
options: Fresh frozen plasma alone over 6 hours
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K
Protamine sulfate given by slow infusion
Tranexamic acid alone at a standard dose
items.explanation: Warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage requires rapid correction of coagulopathy. Prothrombin complex concentrate normalizes the international normalized ratio within minutes with small volume, and vitamin K sustains the effect after the factors wear off. Plasma corrects slowly and requires large volumes. Protamine reverses other anticoagulants and not vitamin K antagonists. Tranexamic acid alone does not replace the depleted clotting factors.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with asthma has a bilateral postural hand tremor that interferes with writing and holding a cup. Her father had a similar tremor. A nonselective beta blocker is contraindicated. Which drug is a reasonable first choice?
items.explanation: A familial, symmetric postural and kinetic tremor without other signs is essential tremor. Propranolol and primidone are the first-line agents, and primidone is chosen when asthma precludes a nonselective beta blocker. It is started at a low dose to limit sedation and nausea. Levodopa is for parkinsonian rest tremor and is ineffective here. Trihexyphenidyl and amantadine are used mostly for parkinsonian or drug-induced syndromes.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had one episode of optic neuritis. Magnetic resonance imaging shows lesions in the periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial regions, but no enhancing lesion. Which finding would satisfy dissemination in time and allow diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
options: Oligoclonal bands present only in the cerebrospinal fluid
A markedly elevated serum neurofilament light chain concentration
Positive serum aquaporin-4 antibody in a high titer
Delayed latency on visual evoked potentials of the affected eye
items.explanation: Under current diagnostic criteria, a single clinical attack with dissemination in space on imaging can be completed by dissemination in time, shown by simultaneous enhancing and nonenhancing lesions, a new lesion, or cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands. Neurofilament light is a nonspecific injury marker. Aquaporin-4 antibody points to a different disease. Evoked potential delay shows optic pathway involvement but not new disease activity over time.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has been taking riluzole for 1 year. She now reports morning headaches, daytime sleepiness, and orthopnea, with a forced vital capacity of 48 percent predicted. Which intervention is most likely to prolong her survival?
options: Coenzyme Q10 at a high daily dose
Lithium carbonate with serum level monitoring
items.explanation: Nocturnal hypoventilation symptoms and a reduced vital capacity signal respiratory muscle failure, the usual cause of death in this disease. Noninvasive ventilation improves survival and quality of life beyond riluzole. Coenzyme Q10 failed to show benefit in a controlled trial. Immune globulin has no role because the disorder is not an immune neuropathy. Lithium was studied after an early signal and later trials were negative.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has episodes of rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, and lip smacking with amnesia. She has had two adequately dosed antiseizure medications fail over 2 years, and magnetic resonance imaging shows left hippocampal sclerosis. What is the best next step?
options: Addition of a third antiseizure medication at the maximal tolerated dose
Placement of a vagus nerve stimulator as the initial procedure
Trial of the ketogenic diet for 3 months
Referral to a comprehensive epilepsy center for presurgical evaluation
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriate drug trials defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance of seizure freedom with a third drug is low. Mesial temporal sclerosis with concordant semiology is the best surgical substrate, and resection offers freedom from seizures in a majority of patients. Neurostimulation is reserved for those who are not resection candidates. Dietary therapy is mainly used in children and generalized syndromes. Referral should not wait for further trials.

items.stem: After rising from a nap, a 55-year-old man reports vertigo, hoarseness, and trouble swallowing, with loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body. Which structure explains the left facial sensory loss?
options: Left spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus
items.explanation: A lateral medullary infarction from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion produces ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss and contralateral body loss. The spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus, which carry pain and temperature from the face, lie in the lateral medulla and are damaged on the same side. The spinothalamic tract has already crossed and explains the body deficit. The principal nucleus lies in the pons, and the medial lemniscus carries vibration and proprioception.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has rigidity, seizures, and school decline. His father developed chorea at age 40, and testing shows a very large CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene. Which mechanism best explains the early onset?
options: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy transmitted through the mother
Skewed X-chromosome inactivation in the affected parent
Further repeat expansion during paternal transmission
items.explanation: Huntington disease shows anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission, because the CAG repeat is unstable during spermatogenesis and often expands. Larger repeats cause earlier onset, and juvenile cases present with rigidity, seizures, and cognitive decline rather than chorea. The gene lies on chromosome 4 and is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, so mitochondrial, disomy, and X-inactivation mechanisms do not apply.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has 2 years of progressive proximal weakness and now needs a wheelchair at night because of orthopnea. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and muscle biopsy shows vacuoles filled with periodic acid-Schiff positive material. Which enzyme is deficient?
items.explanation: Adult-onset proximal weakness with early diaphragm involvement and glycogen-filled vacuoles indicates Pompe disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Enzyme replacement therapy slows decline. Muscle phosphorylase deficiency causes McArdle disease with exertional cramps and myoglobinuria. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency causes exertional rhabdomyolysis after fasting. Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency is often incidental and does not produce this picture.
